PWY-6993.name: nicotine degradation II (pyrrolidine pathway)
PWY-6993.comment:
Nicotine is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum and Nicotiana rustica) [Schmeltz77], where it functions as a defense compound. In the plant tissue nicotine is mostly present in the (S)-nicotine isomeric form [Armstrong98], although tobacco smoke contains up to 10% of (R)-nicotine, probably due to racemization during combustion (in [Hukkanen05]).

Early studies of nicotine degradation by Pseudomonas species identified several intermediates, including pseudooxynicotine, methylamine, 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanoate and 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine [Tabuchi55, Wada57]. The latter was predicted to be further metabolized by cleavage at the 3 position to form 2,5-dihydroxypyridine and succinate semialdehyde [Kaiser96]. 2,5-dihydroxypyridine is believed to be further degraded into the central metabolite fumarate via maleamate and maleate [Wang07b].

The genetics of the system began to clarify upon the study of the aerobic soil bacterium Pseudomonas putida S16, isolated in China, which is able to grow on nicotine as a sole source of carbon and nitrogen [Wang04b]. The genes encoding the enzymes required for nicotine degradation reside in the core genome and in a genomic island [Yu11a]. The first genes were identified by transforming an Escherichia coli strain with a genomic library prepared from Pseudomonas putida S16. Among the three reading frames identified was the hspA gene, which was shown to encode a 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine hydroxylase [Tang08], and the nicA1 gene, which encodes a nicotine dehydrogenase [multifunctional] that was reported to catalyze multiple reactions, transforming (S)-nicotine to 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanoate via N-methylmyosmine [Tang09a]. A gene encoding a second 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine hydroxylase was subsequently discovered outside the nic cluster [Tang11].

The last holes in the pathway were filled after the genome sequencing of Pseudomonas putida S16. A second nicotine dehydrogenase, encoded by the nicA2 gene, was discovered, along with three genes that encode a cytidylyl molybdenum cofactor-dependent 3-succinoylpyridine monooxygenase complex [Tang13].

While the NicA1 protein was reported to catalyze the conversion of N-methylmyosmine to 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanoate in a single step, a study of another nicotine-degrading strain, Pseudomonas sp. HZN6, revealed a different route via 4-oxo-4-(pyridin-3-yl)butanal, which involved two novel enzymes [Qiu12a]. These two enzymes are also present in the genome of Pseudomonas putida S16, and one of them, EC 1.4.3.24, pseudooxynicotine oxidase, has been shown to be essential for nicotine degradation in this organism [Tang13], suggesting that the actual pathway involves all of these enzymes.

CPLX-8439.name: 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine hydroxylase
CPLX-8439.comment:
6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine hydroxylase was purified to homogeneity from Pseudomonas putida S16, and found to be a homodimeric protein of 80 kDa [Tang11]. The N-terminal amino acid sequence was obtained and used to identify the hspB gene that encodes it. The gene is located 30 kb away from the nic gene cluster, which contains the hspA gene. While both genes encode proteins that catalyze the same reaction, they share no sequence similarity.

Deletion of hspB, but not of hspA, blocks nicotine degradation.

The enzyme contains one FAD molecule per monomer, and requires NADH for activity.

CPLX-8990.name: maleate isomerase
CPLX-8990.comment:
A gene cluster named nic2 was described from the nicotine degrading bacterium Pseudomonas putida S16. The cluster contains genes encoding 5 enzymes that catalyze the late steps of the nicotine degradation pathway, mediating the conversion of 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine to fumarate [Tang12].

The maiA gene encodes a maleate isomerase. The gene was cloned and overexpressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity [Tang12].

The purified enzyme catalyzed the last step in the nicotine degradation pathway, the cis-trans isomerization of maleate to fumarate. The enzyme's activity was determined by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) [Tang12].

The gene was later cloned with both N- and C-terminal His-tags and expressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity and crystallized by the hanging-drop vapour-diffusion method. In addition, a C200A mutant was also purified, and crystallized in complex with maleate. The enzyme was shgown to form a homodimer [Chen13].

The structure of the wild type enzyme was determined to 2.95 Å resolution. The structure of the mutant enzyme in complex with maleate was determined to 2.10 Å resolution. The structures reveal that Asn17 and Asn169 play critical roles in recognizing the substrate. It was also found that the maleate is completely buried inside the enzyme's cavity [Chen13].

CPLX-8991.name: 3-succinoylpyridine monooxygenase complex
CPLX-8991.comment:
The mRNA and protein products levels of the spmA and spmC genes were highly expressed in Pseudomonas putida S16 following nicotine induction. The fact that these two genes flank a third gene, spmB, and that the three gene products show significant sequence identities with the subunits of some members of the xanthine dehydrogenase family, suggested that they may encode the three subunits of the 3-succinoylpyridine monooxygenase complex, the last enzyme in the nicotine degradation pathway in this organism with no known genes [Tang13].

A mutant with a polar mutation in spmA was constructed, and could not grow with nicotine as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, confirming that the SpmABC proteins are involved in the pathway. Furthermore, the mutants accumulated 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanoate, suggesting that the genes indeed encode a 3-succinoylpyridine monooxygenase complex. Complementation of the mutant with intact version of the genes restored oxygenation of 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanoate and growth on nicotine [Tang13].

MONOMER-19247.name: N-formylmaleamate deformylase
MONOMER-19247.comment:
A gene cluster named nic2 was described from the nicotine degrading bacterium Pseudomonas putida S16. The cluster contains genes encoding 5 enzymes that catalyze the late steps of the nicotine degradation pathway, mediating the conversion of 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine to fumarate [Tang12].

The nicD gene encodes a N-formylmaleamate deformylase. The gene was cloned and overexpressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity| [Tang12].

Because the substrate N-formylmaleamate was not commercially available, it was chemically synthesized and used for an in vitro assay with the purified protein. Production of maleamate was confirmed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Activity was measured through production of formate by a coupled reaction with NAD-dependent formate dehydrogenase [Tang12].

MONOMER-19248.name: 2,5-dihydroxypyridine dioxygenase
MONOMER-19248.comment:
A gene cluster named nic2 was described from the nicotine degrading bacterium Pseudomonas putida S16. The cluster contains genes encoding 5 enzymes that catalyze the late steps of the nicotine degradation pathway, mediating the conversion of 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine to fumarate [Tang12].

The nicX gene encodes a 2,5-dihydroxypyridine dioxygenase. The gene was cloned and overexpressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity. The purified enzyme was characterized, and shown to oxygenate 2,5-dihydroxypyridine to N-formylmaleamate, as shown by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Enzymatic activity was markedly increased by Fe2+ [Tang12].

The nicX gene was deleted. Resting cells of the gene deletion mutant degraded nicotine, but could not degrade 2,5-dihydroxypyridine [Tang12].

MONOMER-19249.name: maleamate amidohydrolase
MONOMER-19249.comment:
A gene cluster named nic2 was described from the nicotine degrading bacterium Pseudomonas putida S16. The cluster contains genes encoding 5 enzymes that catalyze the late steps of the nicotine degradation pathway, mediating the conversion of 6-hydroxy-3-succinoyl-pyridine to fumarate [Tang12].

The nicF gene encodes a maleamate amidohydrolase. The gene was cloned and overexpressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity| [Tang12].

The purified enzyme transformed maleamate to maleate with the production of ammonium. Activity was measured via monitoring ammonium concentration by a decrease in the amount of NADPH in a reaction buffer containing EC 1.4.1.4, glutamate dehydrogenase (NADP+).

MONOMER-19250.name: nicotine dehydrogenase
MONOMER-19250.comment:
The nicA2 gene of Pseudomonas putida S16 was discovered by analyzing genes whose protein products were increased during growth on nicotine [Tang13].

The gene was cloned and expressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant host gained the ability to convert (S)-nicotine to N-methylmyosmine, confirming that nicA2 encodes a nicotine dehydrogenase. The gene was cloned with a His6 tag and expressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity and found to contain an FAD cofactor [Tang13].

Interestignly, a mutant with a deleted nicA2 gene was not able to grow on (S)-nicotine, even though the nicA1 gene encodes a protein with a similar function.

Acceptor.name: an oxidized electron acceptor
Acceptor.comment:
In general, an electron acceptor is a chemical entity that can accept electrons from another chemical entity. By accepting the electrons, the acceptor is reduced, and thus prior to receiving the electrons the entity is called "an oxidized electron acceptor" and after receiving them it is called "a reduced electron acceptor".

Many reduced electron acceptors are able to transfer the electrons to other molecules, becoming oxidized in the process. Thus the distinction between an electron acceptor and an electron donor is often not determined by the actual chemical entity, but by the role it plays in a particular reaction. However, some acceptors in biological reactions only accept electrons and do not transfer them further. Those are often known as "terminal electron acceptors".

While in general every chemical reaction in which electrons are transferred includes an electron donor and an electron acceptor, several molecules are commonly used in metabolism solely for the purpose of electron transfer, and are referred to in biology as electron acceptors. Different biological electron acceptors differ in the number of electrons that they transfer and in their electron affinity.

Some of the common biological electron acceptors transfer only a single electron (e.g. cytochromes, blue copper proteins, and some ferredoxins), some transfer two electrons (e.g. some ferredoxins), some transfer a hydride ion ( e.g. NAD+ and NADP+), and some transfer two electrons and two protons (quinones, FAD and FMN). In addition, a number of inorganic small molecules (e.g. oxygen, nitrate, iron (III), manganese (IV), sulfate) are often used as terminal electron acceptors.

This particular entry is used for unknown acceptors that transfer two electrons and two protons.

CPD0-1882.name: cytidylyl molybdenum cofactor
CPD0-1882.comment: The name MoO2(OH)Dtpp-mCDP has been suggested as the systematic name for this compound [Fischer98a].

texts.value: Involved in nicotine degradation (PubMed:24204321, PubMed:26237398, PubMed:29812904, PubMed:33432238). Catalyzes the conversion of nicotine to N-methylmyosmine (PubMed:24204321, PubMed:29812904, PubMed:33432238, PubMed:33464876). N-methylmyosmine undergoes spontaneous hydrolysis to form pseudooxynicotine (PN) (PubMed:24204321). S-nicotine is the optimal substrate (PubMed:29812904). Has lower activity with some nicotine analogs, but shows no activity towards neurotransmitters, including serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine, nicotine metabolites and common neuroactive drugs (PubMed:29812904). The enzyme is stereospecific with poor activity with (R)-nicotine as the substrate (PubMed:29812904). The c-type cytochrome protein CycN is the physiological electron acceptor (PubMed:33432238). O(2) is a poor electron acceptor (PubMed:33432238, PubMed:33464876)

reaction.name: (S)-nicotine + 2 Fe(III)-[cytochrome c] = N-methylmyosmine + 2 Fe(II)-[cytochrome c] + 2 H(+)

texts.value: Binds 1 FAD per subunit.
The catalytic rate is not significantly affected by pH

kcat is 0.00664 sec(-1) with O(2) as electron acceptor (at room temperature) (PubMed:26237398). kcat is 0.0132 sec(-1) with O(2) as electron acceptor (at 37 degrees Celsius) (PubMed:26237398). kcat is 0.00611 sec(-1) with O(2) as electron acceptor (at 22 degrees Celsius) (PubMed:29812904).
Optimum temperature is 70 degrees Celsius.
Alkaloid degradation; nicotine degradation
Monomer in solution (PubMed:27933790, PubMed:32873764). Homodimer in solution (PubMed:33432238). Forms homodimers in the crystal (PubMed:32873764, PubMed:33464876)
Expression is up-regulated in the presence of nicotine

Ligand binding is accompanied by structural changes, including puckering of the flavin isoalloxazine ring and closure of a putative substrate entrance tunnel (PubMed:29812904). The product exit passage is blocked by nine bulky amino acid residues (PubMed:32873764). NicA2 has probably evolved a restricted PN exit passage to prevent its accumulation in the cells at an undesirable rate (PubMed:32873764). Replacing the bulky residues at the product exit passage by amino acids with smaller side chains effectively increases the catalytic turnover rate (PubMed:32873764)
Predicted to be exported by the Tat system. The position of the signal peptide cleavage has not been experimentally proven
Deletion of the gene prevents nicotine catabolism

Could be used as a potential therapeutic for the degradation of the critically addictive component in tobacco, nicotine (PubMed:26237398, PubMed:30041697). May decrease nicotine's circulation through its destruction so that an effective concentration is not reached or maintained in the brain (PubMed:26237398). NicA2 rapidly reduces blood and brain nicotine concentrations when administered to rats at single or multiple nicotine doses relevant to the nicotine intake of cigarette smokers (PubMed:30041697)

Overexpression of the gene has a modest toxic effect on cell growth, suggesting that the reaction product pseudooxynicotine (PN) is toxic for the bacteria (PubMed:32873764). Coexpression of Pnao, which converts PN to 3-succinoylsemialdehyde-pyridine (SAP), can rescue the growth of bacteria by alleviating the toxic effects of PN (PubMed:32873764)
Belongs to the flavin monoamine oxidase family

Given NicA2's homology to flavin-dependent amine oxidases, which transfer their electrons directly to O(2), it was assumed that NicA2 is a nicotine oxidase. However, catalytic turnover for NicA2 using O2 as a substrate is extremely slow compared to other enzymes in the amine oxidase family, suggesting that this enzyme is not an oxidase (PubMed:33432238, PubMed:33464876). It was shown later that NicA2 is actually a dehydrogenase, using a cytochrome c as the natural electron acceptor (PubMed:33432238)

Involved in nicotine degradation (PubMed:26634650, PubMed:35835223). Catalyzes the deamination of pseudooxynicotine to 3-succinoylsemialdehyde-pyridine (PubMed:26634650, PubMed:35835223). Functions as a dehydrogenase that uses the c-type cytochrome protein CycN as the physiological electron acceptor (PubMed:35835223). O(2) is a poor electron acceptor (PubMed:35835223). Pnao is oxidized by CycN 230 times faster than O(2) at equivalent oxidant concentrations (PubMed:35835223)
